definition: Stretching part of a fast-moving character or object in the direction of travel — independent of squash & stretch's weight/force purpose — specifically to bridge large per-frame spacing gaps so the eye can track motion that would otherwise read as a hard jump between positions.
purpose: Keep a very fast action visually trackable and legible at low frame density, borrowing squash & stretch's deformation vocabulary for a readability purpose rather than an emotional/force one.
visible_effect: A limb, weapon, or whole silhouette elongated along the motion path for one or two frames during a fast action, similar in appearance to motion blur but achieved as a drawn/posed deformation rather than a rendered blur.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Without it, a fast action sampled at large spacing gaps can read as a discontinuous jump or a skipped frame; with it, the same sparse spacing reads as one continuous fast motion, independent of whether the action itself communicates weight or power.
physical_interpretation: An imitation of real motion blur (the way a fast-moving object blurs across an exposure), not a claim about the object's own elasticity the way squash & stretch's deformation normally is.
use_cases: a very fast attack or ability animation sampled at large spacing gaps, where the pose-to-pose jump would otherwise be hard to track
a stylized 2D or sprite-based game already using squash & stretch as part of its visual language, where a smear reads as consistent with the rest of the style
bridging a gap for a weapon or effect trail specifically, independent of whether the wielding character deforms at all
non_use_cases: a realistic 3D character where the effect would call attention to itself as a drawing convention rather than reading as natural
an action already sampled densely enough (or moving slowly enough) that the spacing gap it exists to bridge is not actually present
confusing this with squash & stretch's core force/weight purpose — a smear can exist on an object the animator explicitly does NOT want to look elastic or soft
interactions: Squash & stretch — borrows its deformation vocabulary for a different purpose (readability, not weight); the existing `squash_stretch` entry's volume-preservation convention does not necessarily apply here, since a smear is read as a motion trail rather than the object's own body
Slow in/slow out — the spacing-gap problem this technique solves is exactly what unevenly-spaced fast motion produces in the first place

Arcs — video 1's independent, uncredited b-roll citation of a 2013 GDC talk on "smears" for hand-drawn animation describes the same technique from a different source, for the same underlying spacing problem

style_variations.anime: a smear is close to a default idiom for a fast strike, consistent with the style's general willingness to break literal continuity for clarity
style_variations.realistic: rendered motion blur (a camera/shader effect) is the expected tool instead; a drawn/posed smear would read as a stylistic anomaly

cadence_representation: Not represented, and not straightforwardly representable: like squash & stretch generally, Cadence has no mesh deformation, so a literal smeared silhouette is not achievable on a rigid Motor6D rig; a pose-based approximation (extending a limb's reach at the smeared frame) is conceivable but would not produce a comparable visual effect the way the pose-based squash/stretch equivalent does for weight, since a smear's whole effect depends on an elongated SILHOUETTE, which Cadence cannot generate without mesh scale.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Indirectly: `ai/motion.js` already measures per-frame spacing (the acceleration/velocity curve slow_in_slow_out relies on), so a phase with unusually large positional gaps between consecutive keys — a candidate for needing this technique — is identifiable from existing data; nothing currently flags "this gap is large enough that a smear would help," since Cadence has no way to add one anyway.
generation_or_modification_methods: None — no mesh deformation exists to generate a smear with, per `cadence_representation` above.
failure_modes: applying a smear to a character or style where it reads as a technical artifact rather than an intentional convention
using a smear to paper over spacing that should instead be fixed with more/better-placed keys or a slow_in_slow_out adjustment
smearing an object whose whole point is to look rigid or heavy, undermining that read
roblox_considerations: No mesh deformation exists in Roblox's standard avatar/Motor6D pipeline either, so this technique is no more reachable there than in Cadence directly; a VFX trail effect (a particle or beam trailing the fast-moving part) is the closer Roblox-native substitute, which is a `ai/vfxspec.js` concern, not a rig-pose one.
performance_implications: None beyond whatever a VFX-trail substitute would cost, which is outside this entry's scope.
examples: stretched weapon and limb trails on fast attacks in Overwatch and League of Legends, named directly as the reason those games' fast actions stay readable despite large spacing gaps (video 4 @ 3:04–3:20)

an elongated, streaked, swirl-shaped silhouette during a fast spin move in a 2D animated cutscene shown later in the same video, visually confirming the same technique from a third example beyond the two named games (video 4 @ ~7:44–7:49)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/1kFRU_xBZnE @ 3:04–3:20 — Dan names the technique and both games directly; a matching visual example (not explicitly narrated as the same technique) appears later in the video's closing 2D-game montage at ~7:44–7:49; independently corroborated by an uncredited GDC-talk citation observed in video 1 of this same batch (see W01-notes.md, video 1 section); experimental until validated
